Senses.Explanation: Coming together through conditions describes contributors combining so that something arises. Hongzhi Zhengjue places the phrase beside a shadow arising from form and an echo from sound. Yinyuan Longqi contrasts birth through conditions coming together with cessation through their separation, while Huiyan Zhizhao compares a lineage's growth to a seed sprouting when conditions combine. Other cited passages use the phrase while discussing whether such combinations possess any independent, fixed basis.

Senses.Explanation: A far-past measure — since the vast great kalpas — ruled at the root in the blood-lineage treatise's unborn mind, and turned to count births, silences, seeds, parents, kicks, and the faceless across eight centuries of halls, letters, and odes. The root sits in the blood-lineage treatise attributed to the first patriarch: was it your own body in the dream? no different — then this body is your own truth-body, this truth-body your own basic mind; and this mind, since the beginningless vast great kalpas, no different from now: never born, never dying, neither more nor less, neither foul nor clean, no coming, no going, no right and wrong, no male or female, no monk or lay, no sage, no commoner, no buddha, no being, no cultivating, no cause and fruit — like empty sky, beyond taking and leaving; through the five-skandha mountain and across the birth-death river, no karma can bind this body; Dahui Zonggao, writing to the official Zeng who calls his own worldly life a great guilt, reads the terror itself as depth: had he not, since the beginningless vast great kalpas, served true good teachers and soaked in the seed-of-wisdom knowing, how could he shake so?; what you call the great guilt even the sages could not escape — knowing all hollow, turn the heart into this gate, wash the stain with the water of wisdom, cut once below the feet and raise no continuing thought; Yuansou Xingduan, instructing the Tiantai trainee whose name is Unstained and whose number Dust-Cut, sets the wheel turning: since the vast great kalpas, birth after birth, death after death, like the whirling fire-wheel, no rest, like the well-rope wheel, high and low by turns — all from losing one's own basic mind, shaming one's own basic nature, chaining to every object, grasping at every dust, head out and head under, never knowing it wrong; and Chushi Fanqi, oding the ninth ancestor of the western line: since the vast great kalpas, never once preached a word — who says that only after five thousand years the lips first parted?; spoken or unspoken, do not slander the ancestors: a broken chopstick churning the great sea, a lamp-wick propping Sumeru. Wuyi Yuanlai, back from the grave-visit, ninety days away from the mountain — who is the one able to leave?; no world beyond mind, only fools divide — brothers, the world knows one lifetime's body, one lifetime's parents, one lifetime's place, and does not know that the parents who bore and the places of every single birth-body, since the vast great kalpas, outrun all counting by wit and strength; repay grace with grace and the great grace cannot be repaid — only not seeing a repayer begins the ever-abiding, and so the bodhisattvas borrow this worldly filiality to work the unconditioned kindness and the unblocked grief; Foyuan Chegang, in the ode for his teacher Tian-tong Yuanwu: eye straight at the crown of the head, the upward raw-iron thorn-burr; yielding nothing to buddha or ancestor, shaking the five peaks; three mountains in his grip, caught and released — the shifting foot that kicked the Tong-pass to shards, beyond measure since the vast great kalpas; seizing the food and driving the plow-oxen, that every one slip the wheel; drawing the nails and knocking the wedges, that every one return to the way's abundance — eating rice without biting grain, wearing cloth without once hanging floss; and Jingting Dezong, asked to the face what the buddha is, answers: no face since the vast great kalpas; what is the ancestor? — this side of now, not yet seen; the monk bows, thanks the teacher, and is warned: do not take it on blindly; then to the hall the pair is given again: the basic mind, ice in fire; the basic nature, a lamp in water; no face since the vast great kalpas, this side of now not yet seen — not yet seen: the mutual mirroring cut off, the whole realm plain with nothing showing, the winter lotus fragrant in the twelfth-month snow.

Senses.Explanation: “A pearl rolling on a tray” is a lively image of activity turning readily without sticking. Hongzhi Zhengjue mirrors the words in one comment—‘tray rolls bright pearl; pearl rolls on tray.’ Yuanwu Keqin gives both directions, says the motion does not fall into emptiness for an instant, and elsewhere asks how such turning could be dead-still or lodged. Xiatang Huiyuan applies the image to speaking Yunmen Chan; before Emperor Xiaozong he expands it as rolling and lively, with no lodging. Chushi Fanqi supplies the other side: even if someone understands old and current teachings with pearl-on-tray fluency, Chushi says that person has still not passed beyond the aggregates. The simile names agility and responsiveness, not by itself the outcome of the surrounding case.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB294.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liangting Ting of Yunxi. Liangting Jingting raises Magu circling Zhangjing's teaching seat three times, shaking his staff and standing still. Zhangjing approves. Repeating the performance at Nanquan, Magu is rejected and asks why the two teachers differ. Nanquan replies that Zhangjing is right but Magu is not: this is moved by the wind's force and will decay. Liangting calls approval and rejection an alternating lifting and pressing, yet also credits Magu with drawing out Nanquan's complete account. His final question asks whether the water buffalo too decays. The headword is Nanquan's quoted distinction, not Liangting's final verdict that one outward gesture is always wrong.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB298.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shenfeng Xian. His verse follows the staff-bearing traveler until a floating cloud hides Chang'an. The headword retains Nanquan's exact quoted voice, while Yikui challenges the present assembly to move beyond passive acceptance of the case's judgments. The cloud image does not conclusively identify which earlier teacher was right.
